messages.subject: non-convergence with a complex hierarchical distribution
parts:
I am trying to fit a non-standard hierarchical model with the help of stan, but having some trouble. Basically, I would like to fit a hierarchical model similar to the 8 schools example from stan, except that rather than placing a hierarchical distribution on the random effects parameters, I want place the hierarchical distribution on the squared random effects parameters.

Why? You can think of the lower level parameters as a bunch of distances, measured for a bunch of different units. Within a unit, the sign on the distance has meaning (e.g., B-A > 0 implies B > A). But once we start averaging across units, the sign has no meaning, because for the first unit, I could calculate B-A or A-B, for the second unit, I could calculate C-D or D-C, etc. I want an estimate that looks at the overall magnitude of the errors, but doesn't depend on direction. Thus, the squaring. I thought if I put a Gamma distribution on the squared random effect parameters, then I could think of the estimated mean of the hierarchical distribution as the mean squared distance (or MSE). But after lots of tinkering with stan, I can't make it converge.

Here is my stan model (also attached):
data {
  int<lower=0> J; // number of units
  real d[J]; // estimated distances
  real<lower=0> sigma[J]; // s.e. of distance estimates
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> mu;
  real<lower=0> tau;
  real theta[J];
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> alpha;
  real<lower=0> beta;
  real<lower=0> theta2[J];
  alpha <- (mu/tau)^2;
  beta <- mu/(tau^2);
  for (j in 1:J)
    theta2[j] <- theta[j]^2;
}
model {
  for(j in 1:J){
    theta2[j] ~ gamma(alpha, beta);
    increment_log_prob(log(fabs(2*theta[j])));
  }
  d ~ normal(theta, sigma);
}

And my data (I made all the distances positive, since sign is meaningless across units):

dat <- list(J = 16,
            d = c(0.551, 0.275, 0.307, 0.372, 0.165, 0.183, 0.656, 0.131, 0.632, 0.042, 0.003, 0.260, 0.488, 0.017, 0.130, 0.227),
            sigma = c(1.322, 0.179, 1.445, 0.565, 0.258, 1.231, 0.457, 0.648, 1.126, 0.590, 0.300, 0.351, 0.324, 0.394, 0.659, 0.441))

And my call to stan from R:

fit.squared <- stan(file = 'meta_squared.stan', data = dat, iter = 10000,
                    control = list("adapt_delta" = .9, "max_treedepth" = 10))

I realize that my estimates are super noisy, and anything I estimate is going to be full of noise (that's part of what I am trying to show in doing this analysis), but the results I get are crazy:

parts:
On Friday, May 27, 2016 at 1:22:30 PM UTC-4, jmf wrote:
I am trying to fit a non-standard hierarchical model with the help of stan, but having some trouble. Basically, I would like to fit a hierarchical model similar to the 8 schools example from stan, except that rather than placing a hierarchical distribution on the random effects parameters, I want place the hierarchical distribution on the squared random effects parameters.
I would declare the squared parameters as primitives with a lower bound of zero

parameters {
  real<lower=0> mu;
  real<lower=0> tau;

real<lower=0> theta2[J];
}

and then take their square roots in the model block

model {
  real theta[J];
  for (j in 1:J) theta[j] <- sqrt(theta2[j]);
  theta2 ~ gamma(alpha, beta);
  d ~ normal(theta, sigma);
}

This way you do not need to make a Jacobian adjustment.

Ben

parts:
Assuming mu and tau don't show up in your model and have the
default uniform positive-constrained priors, then the posterior
is the same as the prior and is improper. The mass is all in
the tail and the "mean" should diverge to +infinity. So Stan's
doing roughly the right thing here, I think.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: non-convergence with a complex hierarchical distribution
parts:
Ok, thanks so much for the input. I went back and thought through the model again and decided to instead model the squared distances directly. I used the delta method to calculate the variance of the squares and then used a gamma model to approximate the sampling distribution. My new model is:

data {
  int<lower=0> J; // number of clinical questions
  real d[J]; // estimated difference in treatment effects
  real<lower=0> sigma[J]; // s.e. of difference estimates
}
transformed data{
  real<lower=0> d2[J];
  for(j in 1:J) d2[j] <- d[j]^2;
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> theta[J];
  real<lower=0> r;
  real<lower=0> lambda;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> mu;
  real<lower=0> alpha[J];
  real<lower=0> beta[J];
  mu <- r/lambda;
  for(j in 1:J) {
    alpha[j] <- (theta[j]/(2*d[j]*sigma[j]))^2;
    beta[j] <- theta[j]/(2*d[j]*sigma[j])^2;
  }
}
model {
  theta ~ gamma(r, lambda);
  d2 ~ gamma(alpha, beta);
}

And it works! Thanks!
